title: Introduction to React
subtitle: Component-based UI — why React, how it works, your first element
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Building complex UIs with raw DOM manipulation (document.getElementById, innerHTML) becomes a maintenance nightmare. State synchronization — keeping the UI in sync with data — requires error-prone manual updates.
whyItExists.solution: React introduces a component model: UI = function(state). You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React handles the DOM updates. When state changes, React re-computes the UI and efficiently updates only the parts that changed (the virtual DOM diff).
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any UI where the page content changes based on user actions or data — dashboards, forms, SPAs, admin panels. React is the industry-standard choice for web UIs at scale.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Static content sites with minimal interactivity (use plain HTML + CSS). Server-rendered pages where SEO matters and JavaScript is minimal (use a framework like Next.js that builds on React, or plain HTML).

explainModes.beginner: React is a library for building user interfaces. Instead of writing code to manually update the page ('find this element, change its text, add this class'), you write components — functions that describe what the UI should look like. When data changes, React automatically updates the page for you.
explainModes.simple: React components are functions that return JSX. ReactDOM.createRoot() mounts your app. React.createElement('div', props, children) creates an element — JSX is syntactic sugar for this. Components compose: one component can render others. State lives in components and drives the UI.
explainModes.standard: The virtual DOM: React maintains an in-memory tree of UI elements. When state changes, React re-renders the component (calls the function), gets a new virtual DOM tree, diffs it against the previous tree, and applies only the minimal set of real DOM changes (reconciliation). This is what makes React fast — DOM updates are batched and minimized. React 18 introduces concurrent features (transitions, Suspense) for better perceived performance.
explainModes.technical: React.createElement(type, props, ...children) is the primitive. JSX compiles to these calls. Fiber: React 18's reconciler is Fiber — a linked list of 'work units' that can be paused, resumed, and prioritized. React.StrictMode runs components twice in development to catch side effects. createRoot replaces render in React 18; createRoot enables concurrent features. Hydration: SSR apps use hydrateRoot to attach React to server-rendered HTML without replacing it.
explainModes.deepDive: The reconciliation algorithm: React uses a heuristic O(n) algorithm rather than the theoretically optimal O(n³) tree diffing. Key assumptions: elements of different types produce different trees (short-circuit — don't try to reconcile them); the key prop identifies stable elements across renders (without keys, React uses position-based matching which can lose state). The Fiber scheduler prioritizes updates: user interactions get higher priority than data fetching; background work can be interrupted. Transitions (startTransition) mark updates as non-urgent so urgent updates (typing) aren't blocked.

questions.question: What does React's virtual DOM do?
options: It stores a backup copy of the HTML for disaster recovery
It keeps an in-memory representation of the UI, diffs it on state changes, and applies only the minimal real DOM updates
It replaces the real DOM entirely — React never touches actual HTML elements
It is an alternative to CSS for styling components
questions.explanation: React maintains a virtual DOM — a lightweight JavaScript representation of the UI tree. When state changes, React re-renders the component (calls the function), produces a new virtual DOM tree, compares (diffs) it with the previous tree, and applies only the specific DOM changes needed. This batching and minimization of real DOM updates is what makes React efficient.

faq.q: Does React replace HTML and CSS?
faq.a: No. React renders HTML elements and you still write CSS. JSX looks like HTML but compiles to JavaScript. React adds a component model and state management on top of the same HTML/CSS you already know. You can use plain CSS files, CSS modules, or CSS-in-JS libraries alongside React.
